score_rationale: FAA publishes a releasable bulk airmen dataset at av-info.faa.gov with pilot first name, last name, city, state, and certificate class — making this B2B-appropriate data with professional license context (analogous to NPPES/NPI practitioner records already in the catalog). The aviation insurance and general aviation services market has clear willingness-to-pay patterns. Score 7 not 8 because the buyer pool is niche relative to healthcare or professional services verticals. Note: this dataset covers individual practitioners (pilots), not businesses — compliance officer should confirm professional-license-as-public-record standard applies as it does for NPPES, bar registries, and contractor licenses.
summary: A cleaned CSV of all FAA-certified airmen (private, commercial, airline transport, and flight instructor certificate holders) sourced from the FAA Releasable Airmen Database — a publicly downloadable file updated monthly at av-info.faa.gov. FAA explicitly releases first name, last name, city, state, country, and certificate type information under its open-data policy. Each record includes the airman's certificate type (student, sport, recreational, private, commercial, ATP), certificate class (airplane single-engine, multi-engine, helicopter, glider, etc.), ratings held (instrument, CFI, CFII, MEI), and state of certificate. Approximately 750,000 active US airmen hold FAA certificates. Aviation insurance companies, flight training academies, private jet charter services, and aviation equipment vendors currently pay list brokers $500–$5,000 for filtered aviation prospect lists built from this exact public data. A one-time $49 flat-file on Gumroad — distinct from the FAA Civil Aircraft Registration dataset already in the catalog — targets an entirely different buyer: the aviation services industry looking for certified pilot prospects, not aircraft owners.

audience.who: Aviation hull and liability insurance companies (Global Aerospace, USAIG, Avemco) who write annual aviation insurance policies for private pilots and need prospect lists filtered by certificate type and state — a commercial pilot cert is a proxy for aircraft ownership, which drives insurance demand; flight schools and aviation academies recruiting for instrument, commercial, and multi-engine add-on rating courses — every private pilot is a warm prospect for the next certificate; charter and fractional ownership operators (Wheels Up, NetJets, charter brokers) recruiting commercial and ATP-rated pilots for their growing operations; luxury aviation services (hangar management, concierge fuel, aviation headhunters) targeting pilots by certificate class and state; avionics and aircraft equipment dealers (Garmin aviation, ForeFlight premium) using pilot lists to run digital and direct mail campaigns.

data_wanted: FAA Releasable Airmen Database — monthly updated bulk file downloadable from https://av-info.faa.gov/. FAA explicitly authorizes release of name, city, state, country, and certificate data. Download page: https://www.faa.gov/licenses_certificates/airmen_certification/releasable_airmen_download/. The download contains two files: (1) PILOT_BASIC.csv — airman unique ID, last name, first name, street (note: FAA omits home street addresses from the releasable file; only city, state, country are included), city, state, zip, country, region, med_class (medical certificate class: 1/2/3), med_date, med_exp_date, (2) PILOT_CERT.csv — airman unique ID, cert_type (student/sport/recreational/private/commercial/ATP), cert_level (flight instructor, ground instructor), ratings string (ASEL, AMEL, instrument, helicopter, glider, CFI, CFII, MEI, etc.). Join on unique ID. Filter for US-address records with at least one active pilot certificate. Target: ~750,000 certified airmen rows after joining and deduplication.

willingness_to_pay.signal: Aviation insurance is a renewals-based business where a single new policyholder pays $800–$5,000/year and churns rarely. A $49 CSV of 750,000 certificated pilots — filterable by certificate type (commercial vs. private) and state — returns its cost in the first one or two new policy quotes. Flight schools have similarly compelling math: a $49 instrument-rating prospect list covering every private ASEL pilot in their state is worth one tuition enrollment ($8,000–$15,000 for a full instrument course). The market gap: no flat-file product exists at this price point. Direct mail list brokers charge $0.05–$0.30 per pilot name (= $37,500–$225,000 for the full dataset). The $49 CSV undercuts by 3–4 orders of magnitude. Compliance note for CEO: FAA explicitly releases names and location in the Releasable Airmen Database; this follows the same professional-license-public-record standard as NPPES and bar registries.
